    • Order flow

    Liquidity heatmap

    A liquidity heatmap shows the resting orders of the order book over time. Price is on the vertical axis, time on the horizontal; the brighter the colour, the more was resting at that price at that moment.

    What is a liquidity heatmap?

    The order book shows one moment. A heatmap records the same book second by second and lines the moments up. You can see when large orders were placed, how long they stayed and what happened as price came near.

    Long bright horizontal lines are large orders resting for a long time (walls). The price line runs between them; big trades and liquidations are often marked on top.

    Marks on the map

    • Wall: a bright line staying at the same price for a long time.
    • Absorption (◆): price leans on a wall, plenty trades into it, yet it does not shrink; it is being refilled or is bigger than it shows.
    • Pulled wall (×): a large order vanished without trading as price came near; most likely cancelled.
    • Circles and squares: big trades (green buy, red sell) and, on futures, liquidations.

    How to read it

    1. Pick out the lasting walls. Walls that stay put for a long time mean more than orders that come and go.
    2. See what happens when price arrives. If the wall melts it is trading, if it vanishes it was pulled, if it stays it is absorbing.
    3. Compare with the zones. A lasting wall inside a Critical Zone means the zone is backed in the book too.

    Three ends of a wall

    Three common cases on the map when price reaches a wall.

    Absorption

    The line stays and much trades on it. Price often pauses at that level.

    Used up

    The line thins as it trades and ends. Price may pass to the other side of the level.

    Pulled

    The line disappears before price gets there. The level's strength is reassessed.

    What it shows, what it does not prove

    What it shows

    • Where large orders rest and since when
    • How walls behave as price comes near
    • When and at which level events such as absorption or pulling happen

    What it does not prove

    • That a wall is a real intention; orders can be cancelled at any moment
    • That price will turn at the wall
    • Orders you cannot see; part of large orders rest in pieces or hidden

    The MarketLevelMap view

    How it relates to zones

    The heatmap on the live flow page draws the Critical Zones of every timeframe as bands and writes each band's timeframe at its left edge. Where zones of several timeframes overlap (e.g. 1D+1W) the band is drawn stronger. A lasting wall and absorption marks inside a zone mean the zone is backed both by past reactions and by today's book.

    Nothing recorded

    The map on the live flow page fills while the page is open; no history is kept. When you open the page it is empty and grows as you watch.

    Often confused with

    • Volume profile (POC, VAH, VAL)A volume profile shows trades that happened; the heatmap shows resting orders that have not traded yet.
    • Sweep: a wick past the range edgeA liquidity sweep is price running quickly through a level where stops rest and coming back; the heatmap shows orders resting in the book.

    Key points

    • The heatmap is the order book over time.
    • Bright horizontal lines are large orders resting for a long time.
    • A wall melting, vanishing or absorbing tells different things.
    • Orders on the map can be cancelled; it does not show direction on its own.
